name: Zuranolone
lead: Zuranolone (brand name Zurzuvae) is an oral neuroactive steroid that acts as a positive allosteric modulator of GABA-A receptors. It is a synthetic analog of the body's own neurosteroid allopregnanolone and was developed by Sage Therapeutics with Biogen. The US FDA approved it in August 2023 for postpartum depression in adults, a 14-day oral course positioned as an alternative to intravenous brexanolone.[1][2][3]

The wiki lists it in the recovery group because neurosteroids are discussed for mood, anxiety and sleep, which feed into how rested, calm and well someone looks and how consistently they train. It has no approved or studied use for appearance. Its US label carries a boxed warning about impaired driving and other hazardous activities, and it is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US.[2][3][4]

In published phase 3 trials in postpartum depression, patients given zuranolone showed greater reductions in depression scores than placebo at day 15. For major depressive disorder, the FDA issued a complete response letter citing insufficient evidence of effectiveness, while Japan approved it for depression in 2026.[5][6][3]
infobox: Neuroactive steroid; GABA-A receptor positive allosteric modulator

paras: The only US-approved indication is postpartum depression (PPD) in adults. The label describes zuranolone as a neuroactive steroid GABA-A receptor positive modulator, taken as a once-daily 14-day course.[2] The European Commission authorised it for PPD in September 2025, and Japan has approved it for depression.[1][3]

Investigational uses reported include bipolar depression, insomnia with depression, essential tremor and Parkinson's disease; registered studies also cover post-stroke depression and adolescent pharmacokinetics.[3][7][8][9]

Zuranolone enhances inhibitory signalling through both synaptic and extrasynaptic GABA-A receptors by binding a neurosteroid site distinct from the benzodiazepine site.[1][10] The label states that how this produces an effect in PPD is not fully understood.[2] Reviews describe neurosteroid GABA-A modulators as a distinct approach from monoaminergic antidepressants.[11][12]

Zuranolone is absorbed orally, with exposure increased by food; it is highly protein-bound and mainly metabolised by CYP3A4, so strong CYP3A4 inhibitors and inducers change its levels. Its half-life is roughly 16 to 25 hours, supporting once-daily dosing, compared with about 9 hours for intravenous brexanolone.[1][3][13]

The label lists somnolence, dizziness, diarrhea, fatigue, nasopharyngitis and urinary tract infection as the most common adverse reactions.[2] A boxed warning states that it causes driving impairment through CNS depressant effects, and advises against driving or hazardous activities for at least 12 hours after a dose during the treatment course.[2]
The label also warns of suicidal thoughts and behaviour, and of possible fetal harm, and describes a pregnancy exposure registry.[2]
Wikipedia lists the formula C25H35N3O2, 99.5 percent protein binding and metabolism via CYP3A4, with an elimination half-life reported as about 16 to 23 hours versus about 9 hours for brexanolone.[3]

Zuranolone (development code SAGE-217) grew out of work on allopregnanolone, whose intravenous form brexanolone was approved in 2019 for postpartum depression and later withdrawn from the US market. Zuranolone was developed as an improvement on the IV neurosteroid, with high oral bioavailability and once-daily use.[3][14]

Sage Therapeutics and Biogen developed it; according to Wikipedia the FDA granted fast track and priority review and approved it in August 2023 for postpartum depression, issuing a complete response letter for major depressive disorder because of insufficient evidence of effectiveness.[3][18] The first-approval review noted the approval was pending scheduling by the DEA, and it is now a Schedule IV controlled substance.[18][3] Wikipedia reports that the EMA committee recommended approval in July 2025, the EU authorised it in September 2025 for adults with postpartum depression, and Japan approved it for major depressive disorder in March 2026; Supernus Pharmaceuticals acquired Sage in 2025, according to Grokipedia.[3][1]

Zuranolone is prescription-only; in the US it is a Schedule IV controlled substance and Canada lists it as prescription-only.[3] Interest in neurosteroids as a class centres on stress, mood and sleep.

The 2021 JAMA Psychiatry phase 3 trial was a double-blind, placebo-controlled study conducted between January 2017 and December 2018 at 27 US sites in women aged 18 to 45 who were six months or fewer postpartum with severe postpartum depression (HAMD-17 of 26 or higher); participants were randomised 1:1 to placebo or 30 mg zuranolone each evening for two weeks, and the primary endpoint was HAMD-17 change at day 15, which favoured zuranolone.[5][3]

A 2023 American Journal of Psychiatry phase 3 trial randomised women with severe postpartum depression to zuranolone 50 mg/day or placebo for a 14-day course and likewise reported greater improvement with zuranolone at day 15.[6] Wikipedia adds that in the two pivotal studies the effect held at day 42.[3] A further analysis examined concurrent anxiety and insomnia symptoms in women with postpartum depression.[19]

In major depressive disorder, the MOUNTAIN phase 3 trial, a later placebo-controlled phase 3 trial and the CORAL study of zuranolone co-initiated with an antidepressant have been published, and a Japanese phase 3 trial appeared in 2026; the FDA declined to approve the MDD indication, citing insufficient evidence of effectiveness, while Japan approved it.[15][16][20][21][3] Reviews describe the neurosteroid class as promising but still being characterised.[11][12][17] Registered studies are testing post-stroke depression and real-world postpartum outcomes.[7][9]

card.summary: Prescription oral neurosteroid approved for postpartum depression; not an appearance compound, and carries a driving-impairment boxed warning.
card.note: Schedule IV in the US with a boxed warning on driving impairment.

quick.overview:
Zuranolone is a prescription capsule taken as a 14-day course for postpartum depression. It is a lab-made relative of allopregnanolone, a steroid the brain makes from progesterone.

It has no studied role in appearance. Its place on the wiki reflects interest in neurosteroids for mood, stress and sleep.
quick.mechanism: It enhances the inhibitory action of GABA at GABA-A receptors through a neurosteroid binding site. The label says the exact way this helps in postpartum depression is not fully understood.
quick.risks: The label has a boxed warning for impaired driving and lists sleepiness, dizziness and fatigue as common effects. It also warns about suicidal thoughts and possible fetal harm. It is prescription-only and a US Schedule IV controlled substance.

chain: Oral neurosteroid enhances GABA-A inhibitory signalling
Depressive symptoms, anxiety and insomnia improve in the studied postpartum population
Better mood and sleep support the rested, healthy look people associate with recovery
angle.text: Zuranolone is a prescription antidepressant for postpartum depression; any link to appearance runs through mood and sleep rather than through the face or body.
